function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repo.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` + `k8s/service.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` |

> **NOTE** – The repo is a simple Node.js “Hello World” app that listens on port **3000** (adjust if your app uses a different port).

---

## 1. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Add the files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this image?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The container starts with `node app.js` – change if your entry point differs.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes manifests

Create a folder `k8s/` and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * The Deployment runs 2 replicas of your app.  
> * The Service exposes the pods on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).  
> * The image name uses GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`). Adjust if you use another registry.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` and add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    # Checkout the repo
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    # Set up Node.js
    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    # Install dependencies
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    # Run tests (optional – remove if you don't have tests)
    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    # Build Docker image
    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

    # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    # Push Docker image
    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **How it works**  
> 1. On every push to `main`, the workflow checks out the repo.  
> 2. It installs Node.js, runs tests, builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, logs into GHCR, and pushes the image.  
> 3. The image name is `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:<sha>` – you can change the tag strategy if you prefer `latest` or a semantic version.

---

## 3. Commit & push the changes

```bash
# Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 4. Verify

1. **Docker** – After the push, the GitHub Actions run will build and push the image.  
   ```bash
   docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>
   ```
2. **Kubernetes** – Apply the manifests to your cluster:
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/
   ```
3. **Service** – Check the service status:
   ```bash
   kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service
   ```

That’s it! Your repo now has a ready‑to‑use Dockerfile, Kubernetes deployment/service, and a CI pipeline that automatically builds and publishes the image whenever you push to `main`.
